reference.source: WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours / Desmoid Tumour Working Group consensus guidance
clinicalPearls: A clonal fibroblastic proliferation that is locally aggressive and infiltrative but has no capacity to metastasise
Sporadic tumours usually carry activating CTNNB1 (beta-catenin) mutations, whereas APC-mutated tumours occur in familial adenomatous polyposis and favour the mesentery

Abdominal wall lesions classically arise in women during or after pregnancy, extra-abdominal tumours around the shoulder girdle and limbs, and intra-abdominal tumours in familial adenomatous polyposis
Nuclear beta-catenin staining supports the diagnosis alongside the characteristic bland spindle cells in a collagenous stroma
Behaviour is unpredictable, with some tumours stabilising or even regressing spontaneously, so active surveillance is now the preferred initial approach for many patients
Systemic options when treatment is needed include tyrosine kinase inhibitors, gamma-secretase inhibition, hormonal manipulation, anti-inflammatory agents, and cytotoxic chemotherapy
Surgery is no longer first-line because of high local recurrence and functional cost, and positive margins do not reliably predict recurrence
A new mesenteric or multifocal desmoid should prompt evaluation for familial adenomatous polyposis, including colonic assessment
reference.pathophysiology: Desmoid tumour is a monoclonal fibroblastic and myofibroblastic neoplasm driven by constitutive activation of the Wnt signalling pathway. In sporadic disease this results from somatic activating mutations in CTNNB1, the gene encoding beta-catenin, which stabilise the protein so that it accumulates and translocates to the nucleus to drive transcription of proliferative target genes. In the setting of familial adenomatous polyposis, germline APC mutations achieve the same downstream effect by removing the negative regulation of beta-catenin. The resulting proliferation of uniform spindle cells within a dense collagenous matrix infiltrates adjacent muscle and fascia along tissue planes, encasing rather than destroying structures. Local factors such as prior surgery, trauma, and the hormonal milieu of pregnancy appear to promote tumour development, consistent with the observed clinical associations, while the absence of metastatic potential reflects the tumour's fibroblastic, non-epithelial biology.
additionalDifferentials: Nodular fasciitis and other benign fibroblastic proliferations
Scar or keloid and reactive fibrosis
Sclerosing mesenteritis or retroperitoneal fibrosis for mesenteric lesions
Superficial fibromatosis when the presentation is palmar or plantar
additionalInvestigations: MRI to define extent, infiltration, and relationship to neurovascular structures and for surveillance
Image-guided core biopsy with histology and beta-catenin immunohistochemistry
CTNNB1 mutation analysis to support diagnosis and prognostication
Colonoscopy and APC testing when familial adenomatous polyposis is suspected
CT of the abdomen for mesenteric or intra-abdominal disease
Baseline functional and pain assessment to guide the decision between surveillance and active treatment
redFlags: Rapid enlargement or new neurovascular compromise from local infiltration
Bowel obstruction, ischaemia, or ureteric obstruction from mesenteric disease
A mesenteric or multifocal tumour indicating possible familial adenomatous polyposis
Tumour encroaching on the airway, spinal canal, or major vessels
Uncontrolled pain or functional loss despite conservative measures
reference.prognosis: Desmoid tumours do not metastasise, and many stabilise or regress under active surveillance, but they cause significant morbidity through local infiltration and have a high propensity for recurrence after surgery. Long-term outcome depends on site, since mesenteric and head and neck lesions can be life-threatening, whereas abdominal wall tumours generally behave more indolently.
pitfalls: Rushing to radical surgery when active surveillance would allow spontaneous stabilisation and preserve function
Assuming a positive resection margin mandates re-excision, as margin status correlates poorly with recurrence
Missing an underlying familial adenomatous polyposis in a patient with a mesenteric desmoid
Mistaking the bland infiltrative spindle cells for a reactive scar or, conversely, for a sarcoma

management: Active surveillance with serial clinical exam and MRI is the preferred first step for asymptomatic newly diagnosed or recurrent desmoid tumours, since outcomes are comparable to immediate treatment
Trigger treatment (systemic therapy, surgery, or radiation) when the patient becomes symptomatic (pain, functional loss, compression, obstruction) or shows clear progression on imaging
Weigh tumour size, site, and younger age as recurrence-risk factors when choosing treatment; microscopic margin status alone should not drive the decision to operate or re-operate

Surgery is reasonable for small resectable abdominal wall tumours and for mesenteric tumours separable from central vessels, but large extremity or chest wall tumours in young patients favour a systemic-therapy-first approach given high recurrence after resection
For systemic therapy, consider anti-inflammatory agents such as sulindac or other NSAIDs first for lower-risk disease given their favourable toxicity profile
Hormonal manipulation such as tamoxifen, gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists, or aromatase inhibitors is an option supported mainly by anecdotal response data
Cytotoxic chemotherapy, including anthracycline-based regimens or combination chemotherapy, is reserved for more aggressive or refractory disease
A multitargeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor improved progression-free survival versus placebo in a randomised trial and is a reasonable option when a more predictable response is needed
A gamma-secretase inhibitor targeting Notch signalling is under investigation as a targeted option in refractory disease
Counsel that systemic therapy responses are typically slow and stable disease should not prompt discontinuation; change treatment for toxicity or clear progression rather than pace of response

Avoid routine postoperative radiation when resection margins are negative; its use with positive margins is debated given radiation risks in a young population and reasonable local control with surgery alone
Consider definitive non-operative radiation as an emerging alternative to surgery when resection would compromise function

Consider image-guided regional or ablative therapies such as high-intensity focused ultrasound, cryoablation, or transarterial chemoembolisation as alternatives to surgery or radiation for selected extra-abdominal desmoids

Evaluate for familial adenomatous polyposis when a mesenteric or multifocal desmoid is found, and refer to a sarcoma multidisciplinary team for management planning, urgent surgical or interventional radiology assessment for obstruction, fistulisation, or compression of vital structures, and genetics/colorectal assessment when FAP is suspected
